body_markdown:
Despite all the marvelous Rolls-Royces made over the years—prewar, postwar, coachbuilt, limousines, cabriolets—my favorite, I must say, is the Silver Shadow. They have a timeless quality I love, and they still turn heads today.


The original Silver Shadow was quite the departure from the ultra-formal Silver Clouds, Silver Wraiths, and Phantoms, with their upright, formal, flowing, and curvy lines. By the mid-1960s, those models were looking rather dated, if still magnificent and gorgeously crafted and appointed.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


As a child of the ’80s and a lover of Matchbox cars, Hot Wheels, and Pocket Cars (how Tomica Japanese diecast models were marketed in the U.S.), I had several mini-me Silver Shadows as a kid, including silver and burgundy Matchbox versions.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


Since I was a sometimes destructive moron little kid, the silver Matchbox one with a harmonious red interior did not last. But the maroon one survives to this day. Circa 1989, I gave it a HORRID flat gold paint job, but I rediscovered it in a box around 2010 and used mineral spirits to remove it and reveal the largely well-preserved original paint.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


And around 1985 or so, my paternal grandmother, Ruby Klockau, would often, during summer break, pick me up and take me to lunch. I always loved those days, and eagerly awaited the appearance of her black 1977 Thunderbird with the white interior and red dash, seatbelts, and carpet. And its original factory AM/FM stereo with CB!


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


And one day we were, likely after lunch at Bishop’s Buffet at South Park Mall, at Toys R Us, and I spied a 1/24 Silver Shadow II in silver by Bburago and had to have it. Grammy was happy to indulge mini-me car nut Klockau. It was very detailed, with opening front doors, hood, and trunk, and the front seats folded forward.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


But I was also a frequently stupid little kid. And eventually I destroyed that Bburago Silver Shadow II, through no fault of its own. It still occasionally bothers me today. But I found a fairly decent one on eBay in the early 2000s, and about ten years ago found a MINT unboxed one at a little antique store in Albany, Illinois. It sits in a Lucite display case on my desk in my home office, to this day.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


So perhaps you now might understand how happy and excited I got when I saw this marvelous 1979 Silver Shadow II at the British Motor Fest in Palatine, Illinois, last September. I had heard of the show from a friend of a friend, who lives in greater Chicagoland, and when I mentioned it to my friend in Texas, Jayson Coombes, he was excited enough to make his annual trip to the Midwest coincide with attending the event.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


There were, in fact, two gorgeous 1979 Silver Shadow IIs at this show—a show I highly recommend if you live within a few hours of Palatine, Illinois. I spent a long time deciding which to bring to you fine folks, and ultimately settled on the example you see here, because owners Dennis and Crystal Klemm, of Wisconsin, were so nice. I was extremely happy that they brought their gorgeous car!


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


I frequently go into a trance when I see a classic car I really love. I guess I was wandering around this car a lot, and apparently Mrs. Klemm noticed as I was hovering over her car and said, “Hey! Go ahead and open the doors if you want!” So I did. And boy, this car was *so* pretty.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


As the seven of you who regularly read my columns know, I am a sucker for luxury cars, foreign or domestic, and I’m especially fond of cars in gorgeous, deep, *actual* colors like red, blue, and green. And the two-tone dark red and burgundy of this RR Silver Shadow II almost made me black out.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


So now I should probably tell you a few facts about the Silver Shadow IIs, other than how much I love them. The II was introduced in February of 1977 and featured many refinements over the original car.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


Among the new features of the Silver Shadow II were power-assisted rack-and-pinion steering (replacing the old recirculating ball version), a deeper Parthenon grille with an air dam below the bumper (said bumpers now being rubber-coated with a chrome trim embellishment on the top), and a revised front suspension that made the car much more driver-friendly.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


Also new, and one of a kind at the time, was a new split-level air conditioning system with automatic climate control. The upper and lower HVAC were completely independent, so you could warm your feet and cool your face at the same time.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


As John Bolster said in his Osprey Auto History book on the Silver Shadow, “…it is the only system which provides completely independent temperature control at both upper and lower levels…” Other Silver Shadow II improvements included dual exhaust with six silencers (U.S. and Japan-bound RRs had catalytic converters instead of the front silencers), an all-new dash with more modern controls, and a transmission lever with integrated cruise control.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


Its wheelbase was 120 inches, overall length 204.5 inches, and width was 71.8 inches. Track was widened over the original Silver Shadow. As usual, under the hood was a 6.75-liter (412-cubic-inch) V-8. As RR had famously stated for many years, power was “adequate.”


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


The V-8 was an aluminum block with 4.1″ by 3.9″ bore x stroke. This refined power plant was backed up by a GM Turbo-Hydramatic 400 3-speed automatic transmission. Top speed, depending on the driver of the day, was 115-118 mph, with zero to sixty occurring in about ten seconds. Impressive for a late-70s large, comfy, and refined British automobile! I’ll always love them.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


Oh, and I couldn’t help myself; I had to include a few pictures of the other 1979 Silver Shadow II.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)


It was equally gorgeous.


[Thomas Klockau](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/tklockau/)
